info.name: lumen — API catalog (§1 public · §8 admin · §9 secrets)
info.description:
**One request per endpoint; every case is an EXAMPLE on that endpoint.**

- Pick an endpoint → the Examples tab lists its documented cases with the REAL captured responses (live dev binary, OpenBao plane, seeded corpus — captured 2026-11-09; ids/timestamps are dev-captured, JWTs truncated).
- Environments: `lumen-dev` / `lumen-staging` / `lumen-production`. The API has NO public ingress ever (INFRA §2) — staging/prod reach via `kubectl -n <ns> port-forward svc/lumen 8080:8080` with baseUrl left at localhost.
- Run `POST /admin/session` once per session: it captures `token`; every admin example inherits `Bearer {{token}}`.
- Dev passwords in this collection/compose are throwaway placeholders; for staging/prod TYPE the admin password at runtime and DO NOT save the environment.

request.description:
Liveness probe: the process answers. No dependencies checked — by design.

**None** — public.

`200` always (if the binary is up). Used by k8s livenessProbe; `/readyz` carries the opinions.

Readiness probe with opinions: Postgres (truth) AND Meilisearch (the read path) must ANSWER, not merely accept TCP.

**None** — public.

`200` ready · `503` engine unreachable (pure-engine posture) or fixture mode (honest `engine not configured`).

response.name: 200 — engine answering
response.comment: 503 shape when the engine is down: `{"error":{"message":"search engine unavailable"}}` — see DESIGN §4.

request.description:
The published feed. **Engine-served** (Meilisearch): `total` is the full filtered count; `items` come in engine order hydrated from Postgres truth. Absent `limit` = the whole corpus.

**None** — public.

| param | type | meaning |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| `tag` | repeated | OR-matched tags (§1) |
| `from`,`to` | `YYYY-MM-DD` | inclusive window on the editorial date |
| `readMin`,`readMax` | int | inclusive minutes window |
| `sort` | `newest`\|`oldest`\|`quickest`\|`longest`\|`relevance` | explicit override; absent = curation (`rank`) |
| `offset`,`limit` | int | pagination; non-numeric → `400` |

`200` · `400` unknown sort or non-numeric paging — *a typo must not pose as curation*.

The `status = published` filter is carried by EVERY query, and hydration re-checks truth at the DB edge — a lagging index can at worst omit a just-committed row, never leak a draft.

request.description:
One post in full: raw Markdown (`content`) with mermaid fences INTACT (Route B — the FE renders it), tags in author order, absolute `thumbnail`.

**None** — public.

`slug` — path segment.

`200` published detail · `404` unknown slug **and every draft/unpublished** — indistinguishable by design.

Point read from truth (not the engine): this is where the leak rule becomes visible — the draft leak-bait IS indexed (the admin door needs it) and still 404s here.

{"slug":"shape-of-a-useful-queue","title":"The shape of a useful queue","subtitle":"Backpressure, fairness, and the promises hidden between producers and consumers","preview":"A practical look at backpressure, fairness, and the costs hidden between producers and consumers. A queue is less a data structure than a set of promises about what happens when systems disagree about speed — and every new producer quietly renegotiates those promises before the first message is ever enqueued.","date":"2024-05-14","readTime":8,"thumbnail":"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1639322537228-f710d846310a?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&fit=max&fm=jpg&w=1080","tags":["distributed-systems","queues","backpressure"],"content":"Queues are not storage with a nicer API. They are a contract between speed, pressure, and time.

## The queue is a promise

A queue absorbs a burst by giving producers and consumers different speeds without pretending that the difference has disappeared. It holds work long enough for a system to make progress at its sustainable rate, turning a sharp arrival pattern into something a worker can handle.

That pause is a contract. When consumers cannot keep up, the queue defines what happens next: work waits, work is dropped, or the producer is asked to slow down. A useful queue makes that decision visible instead of hiding it behind an apparently limitless buffer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Producer] --> Q{{bounded queue}}
  Q --> C[Consumer]
  Q -- full --> BP[backpressure]
  BP -- refuses --> P
```

```mermaid
  participant API as API gateway
  participant Bank
  Customer->>Web: Place order
  Web->>API: POST /orders
  activate API
  API->>Bank: Authorise payment
  Bank-->>API: Approved
  API-->>Web: 201 Created
  deactivate API
  Web-->>Customer: Order confirmed
  Note over Customer,Bank: One order, one transaction
```

Bounded buffers are uncomfortable because they expose the finite nature of the system. Once the buffer fills, the producer has to choose between waiting, retrying, rejecting work, or finding another path. That choice is not an implementation detail; it is the system's response to pressure.

Explicit rejection protects downstream systems from a quiet collapse. It keeps memory use predictable, gives operators a signal they can measure, and lets callers decide whether a request is worth trying again. A queue that never says no is often only postponing the failure.

```go
func (q *Queue) Push(job Job) error {
	if q.full() {
		return ErrBackpressure
	}
	q.items = append(q.items, job)
	return nil
}
```

## Fairness has a cost

FIFO ordering is a clear promise, but it is not always the most useful one. Priority work may need to pass routine work, and once priorities exist, starvation becomes a risk that must be measured and managed. Fairness is a policy with a cost, not a property that appears for free.

> A queue buys time. It does not create capacity.

## A practical checklist

Choose a bound, define the rejection behavior, and make the pressure visible. Decide whether ordering matters more than throughput, then test the queue at the point where consumers fall behind.

```bash
curl -s localhost:8080/metrics | grep queue_depth
```

## Further reading

- [Patterns for distributed systems](https://example.com/distributed-systems)
- [Notes on reliability and failure](https://example.com/reliability)
- [Load shedding in practice](https://example.com/load-shedding)
"}

The editor's document: full draft detail — `content` raw, `tags` in author order, `rev` (the CAS handle for PUT), timestamps, `publishedAt` (null until first publish).

request.description:
The optimistic-locked save: body `{draft: {...}, rev: N}`. `rev` must EQUAL the current value — mismatches touch NOTHING (verified by `RowsAffected`, so even a check-then-write race resolves as 409, never a silent lost update). Success bumps `rev` and enqueues the index job in the SAME transaction (river InsertTx).

**Bearer {{token}}**.

`200` new detail (`rev` +1) · `409` stale rev · `404` gone.

Where does `rev` come from? The last `GET /admin/posts/{slug}` (or the create/update response). It is deliberately NOT an etag header — the client is one author who can read the row.

item.name: Admin — Photos (§8/§5)

request.description:
The upload relay (multipart field `photo`): lumen DECODES the bytes (client type-claims are suggestions — pixels are truth), REBUILDS the image (EXIF and every ancillary chunk die by construction), PUTs a content-addressed key (`media/<sha[:2]>/<sha>.<ext>`) to S3-compatible storage, and commits row + `media_assets` GC ledger + index job in ONE transaction.

**Bearer {{token}}**. In Postman: pick `postman/sample.png` in the Body→file field (paths are machine-local).

`201` AdminPhoto · `415` undecodable or unsupported format (**jpeg|png only** — webp awaits a trusted encoder, recorded not silently dropped) · `413` > 20 MiB · `503` media store not configured.

Fresh photos land `gallery:false, collection:null` — surfacing to the public is a deliberate act (mellon doctrine). `alt` arrives filename-derived; the author edits it.

The darkroom: envelope `{total, items, page, pageSize=24}` over the WHOLE library — non-gallery photos included (the public surface filters those away).

**Bearer {{token}}**.

`collection` repeated (accepts `uncategorized` for NULL), `gallery` `1|0`, `from`/`to` (created_at days), `sort` (`created` default|`title`=alt|`collection`), `dir`, `page` (clamps).

`200`.

item.name: Secrets plane (§9)

request.description:
Enumerate the policy-scoped plane: `kv/metadata` listing → `[{app, env}]`. NAMES ONLY — bytes never ride a list.

**Bearer {{token}}** (lumen's AppRole guards the plane itself; the portal never sees those credentials — THE §9 promise).

`200` · routes ABSENT entirely when lumen has no `LUMEN_BAO_*` env (honest absence — dev: run `make dev-plane`, restart).

Read one secret. `?version=N` pins history (SDK `ReadWithData` — splicing the query into an api path is a 404 waiting to happen). `?meta` answers the version HISTORY (currentVersion + per-version times) instead of values — the CAS handle source.

**Bearer {{token}}**.

`200` payload `{data, createdTime, version, destroyed, deletionTime}` (camelCase — mellon's SecretPayload mirrors it) · `400` malformed version · `404` unknown path.

VALUES ride the response (the UI masks them reveal-on-press) — lumen's LOGS never do: op lines carry path + version + key COUNTS only; the redaction proof lives in the Go battery (`bao_integration_test.go`).

CAS write: `{data, cas}` — `cas` must equal `currentVersion` (`?meta` for the handle); a mismatch is a 409, NEVER a silent clobber. `cas: 0` means create-only. Returns the new version.

**Bearer {{token}}**.

`200 {version}` · `409` stale cas · `400` missing `data`.

response.name: 400 — `data` object required (may be empty — never null)
